NRBS 4210: PROFESSIONAL NURSING PRACTICE OF 
ADUL T CLIENTS III 
O WEN EMMENDORFER, ALE XANDER JONES, NA T ALIA KIMSZA, 
REY NAL DO MAR TINEZ, ROSL Y N PERLES, XUAN, W AN, S T AEL LE ZEPHIR

Risk F actor/ Prevention/ Health Promotion/ Early 
Detection
Risk factors
Early detection: 
focus on recognizing early manifestation Of GBS: 
Symmetric Ascending Weakness: Typically starts 
in the legs and progresses upward.
Reflex Changes: Diminished or absent deep 
tendon reflexes (hyporeflexia or areflexia).
Sensory Disturbances: Paresthesias (numbness, 
tingling) in the hands and feet.
Prevention/Health promotion  
Prevention
Risk Factor/Prevention
• Recent infection: GBS frequently develops 
1–2 weeks after a gastrointestinal (GI) or 
respiratory illness.
• Bacterial infection: Campylobacter jejuni, 
a bacterium that can cause diarrhea, 
common trigger.
• Viral infections: Cytomegalovirus (CMV), 
influenza, HIV, Zika virus, and COVID-19 
have been associated with GBS.
• Prevention: There is no clear main 
preventive measure. Early medical 
assessment and treatment of an acute 
preceding respiratory or gastrointestinal 
infection constitute secondary risk 
reduction. 
Health promotion  
• Respiratory Protection:  In order to predict when 
elective mechanical ventilation may be required, 
breathing patterns and vital capacity are continuously 
monitored.
• Skin Integrity and Mobility: Functional positioning and 
passive range-of-motion exercises twice a day. To avoid 
pressure injuries, shift positions frequently and place 
foam cushioning over bony prominences.
• Communication and Nutrition: Patients with bulbar 
weakness may require gastrostomy implantation or 
enteral assistance. When voice or facial muscles are 
paralyzed, alternative communication methods (such as 
graphic cards or eye-blink techniques) can be used.
• Coping and Fatigue Management: Instruction on how to 
manage fatigue during recovery by planning rest 
intervals and pacing daily activities. Reducing anxiety 
through patient education, family involvement, and 
entertaining activities
Early detection 
Focus on recognizing early manifestation 
including: 
• Symmetric Ascending Weakness: 
Typically starts in the legs and 
progresses upward.
• Decreased/absent reflexes, 
paresthesias, facial/bulbar weakness, 
and respiratory difficulty
• Reflex Changes: Diminished or 
absent deep tendon reflexes 
(hyporeflexia or areflexia).
• Sensory Disturbances: Paresthesias 
(numbness, tingling) in the hands and 
feet.

Clinical Manif estations 
Classic clinical manifestations: 
•  Symmetrically ascending bilateral 
weakness with hyporeflexia, 
dyskinesia, paresthesia, and possible 
respiratory weakness
• Timeline:
⚬ S/s typically present 1-3 weeks 
following the viral/bacterial 
infection or other triggering 
event.
⚬ GBS generally progresses to 
maximum severity within 2-4 
weeks.
Early Signs and Symptoms:
• Diminished reflexes and muscular 
weakness in the lower extremities 
that may progress upward
⚬ Flaccid paralysis 
• Reduced/absent deep tendon 
reflexes
• Paresthesia: usually in the hands 
       and feet
• Demyelination of sensory neurons 
may cause pain
• S/s present bilaterally and 
symmetrically ascend varying by case
Later Signs and Symptoms: 
• Severe respiratory weakness
⚬ 10%-30% of cases
⚬ necessitating mechanical 
ventilation
• Cranial nerve demyelination s/s vary 
by nerve impacted: 
⚬ Optic nerve: possible blindness
⚬ Vagus and glossopharyngeal: 
dysphagia, inability to clear 
secretions
⚬ Vagus nerve: variable autonomic 
dysfunction with s/s inc HTN, OH, 
tachycardia, or bradycardia
⚬ For all: LOC and cognitive 
function are unaffected.

Diagnostic T ests
• A history of viral or bacterial illness within 1-3 weeks with 
clinial manifestations suggest diagnostic testing is needed
• Negative inspiratory force (NIF) meter is used to identify 
neuromuscular respiratory failure
⚬ Reading of > -60 cm H20 is weaker than normal
⚬ Reading of > -30 cm H2O suggests significant 
neuromuscular fatigue
• Lumbar punture with CSF analysis
⚬ Positive result - Albuminocytologic Disassociation
￭ Elevated protein levels and normal WBCs in CSF
• Electrophysiology studies are used to reveal severity of nerve 
dysfunctionality
⚬ Serial tests are used to monitor recovery or progression of 
disease
• Serum Lab tests are not useful in diagnosing GBS
⚬ However, they can be used to identify variant forms or 
atypical symptoms
Nursing Implications f or Lumbar Puncture
Pre-Procedure:
• Verify signed consent and education
• Have patient empty bladder and bowels 
immidiatley prior to procedrure
Intra-Procedure:
• Assist patient into lateral recumbant position 
with knees flexed tightly to abdomen and chin 
to chest
Post-Procedure:
• Assist patient to flat or dorsal recumbant 
position with a pillow under the head
• Encorage hydration and to replenish CSF and 
reduce headache risk

Managing Potential Complications
• Respiratory Failure
⚬ Monitor breathing, O  saturation, and vital capacity; support with intubation & ventilation if needed.₂
• Autonomic Dysfunction (Cardiac arrhythmias, transient HTN, orthostatic hypotension)
⚬ Monitor ECG, administer short‑acting meds for tachycardia/HTN; IV fluids/vasoactive meds for hypotension
• Thromboembolic Events (VTE, DVT, PE)
⚬ Use anticoagulants, sequential compression boots, frequent repositioning, ROM exercises, consult PT and OT
• Bulbar Weakness (Speech & Swallow Dysfunction)
⚬ Assess CN (V, VII, IX, X, XI, and XII), gag reflex, resp. status; implement aspiration precautions, suction at bedside, 
anticipate parenteral nutrition/G tube feeding, consult ST
• Urinary Retention
⚬ Intermittent catheterization, alpha-blocker tamsulosin
• Pressure Ulcers
⚬ Frequent skin assessments and repositioning
Medical Management GBS
Immunotherapy
IVIG or plasma exchange to reduce nerve damage
Pain management 
Treat somatic and neuropathic pain
ICU care
For severe or rapidly progressing GBS

Medication Management & Nursing Responsibilities
Immunotherapy: IVIg 
• IVIg: 
⚬ 0.4 g/kg BW/day, for 5-days
⚬ Pre-Infusion
￭ Assess understanding of Tx, 
PMH infusion reaction, 
breath sounds, fluid status, 
baseline VS, IV access
￭ Edu on adverse reactions
⚬ During-Infusion
￭ Infusion rate 0.5 – 1 
mL/kg/hour initial 15 – 30 
minutes; if no adverse 
reaction → rate can be 
increased every 15 – 30 min 
(max: 3 – 6 mL/kg/hour) 
￭ Monitor VS (BP , RR, fever) 
and for anaphylaxis/infusion 
reaction
⚬ Post-Infusion
￭ Assess for delayed reaction
￭ Reinforce education about 
consecutive day course
￭ Ensure appt (if outpatient) 
scheduled
Supportive Pharmacological Care
• Anticoagulants: heparin, LMWH, or warfarin for DVT prophylaxis
⚬ Monitor platelets, aPTT, PT, INR; monitor for S/S hemorrhage; edu about adverse effects, bleed risk 
precaution, and medication adherence; know drug interaction & antidotes
• Pain Management 
⚬ Analgesics: NSAIDS or acetaminophen, potentially with opioid agents, PRN 
￭ Assess for PMH GI, renal, and hepatic disease; monitor labs and adverse effects; reassess pain; 
edu on reversal agents
⚬ Anticonvulsants: gabapentin (preferred/1st-line) or carbamazepine
￭ Edu on sedation effect; r/f blood dyscrasias with carbamazepine; severe adverse effects = SJS & 
TEN; practice caution w/ PMH renal and hepatic illness; monitor therapeutic level
⚬ Tricyclic Antidepressants: amitriptyline, nortriptyline, or nortriptyline 
￭ Baseline EKG and BP; edu on anticholinergic & sedation effects, suicidal risk, and to not stop 
abruptly; monitor for mood/affect change; drug interaction w/ MOAIs; fall precautions
• Cardiovascular Meds (atropine, short-acting BB, nitroprusside)
⚬ Continuous monitor BP , HR, ECG, resp status; titrate and wean
• Bladder Dysfunction Meds (tamsulosin)
• Monitor BP , HR, orthostatic hypotension, fall precautions
• IV fluids & parenteral nutrition (high energy/cal and high protein)
⚬ Assess IV access and gag reflex; monitor for refeeding syndrome, hyperglycemia, fluid volume 
overload; monitor stool and urine output; mouth care
Supportive Holistic Care
• Improving Communication
⚬ Utilize communication aids, consult speech therapy 
• Decreasing Anxiety
⚬ Educate patient about GBS, coping resources, relaxation/distraction technique, diversional activities, 
social visitation, audiovisual communication, reading sessions, music/audiobooks/TV/movies
• Reducing Fatigue
⚬ Manage energy levels: pacing activities & implementing rest breaks; Identify physically demanding 
activities, assess sleep, assist with self-care, supportive diet

P atient & F amily Education
• Environmental modifications at home 
⚬ Remove rugs, adequate lightening, handrails 
• Adaptive aids for ADLs 
⚬ Wheelchairs, bedside commodes, shower benches 
• Maintaining mobility 
⚬ Passive range of motion exercises
• Caregivers: Proper body mechanics 
⚬ Maintain a wide base of support 
⚬ Keep the patient close during transfers  
• Alarming signs and symptoms to notify emergency services  
⚬ Respiratory failure: 
￭ S/S: Trouble breathing, tachycardia, shortness of breath, use of accessory 
muscles, wheezing 
⚬ Deep Vein Thrombosis (DVT): 
￭ S/S: Redness, warmth, swelling, tenderness, calf pain 
￭ Complication: PE (S/S: sudden chest pain, SOB)  medical emergency→

Discharge Planning & 
Homecare
• Educated the patient and family about the disorder and its usual 
favorable prognosis 
⚬ Treatment focuses on symptom management 
⚬ Patients who experience prolonged paralysis may require 
extensive rehabilitation 
￭ Ventilator dependent 
• Promote mobility 
⚬ Occupational and physical therapy 
⚬ Passive range of motion exercises 
• Education on expected health outcomes 
⚬ Decrease anxiety, enhance physical mobility, effective airway 
clearance 
• Health promotion and screenings 
⚬ Vaccinations (COVID-19, influenza) 
⚬ HIV screenings

Jejuni

E. Epstein-Barr
F. Diabetes
G. Myasthenia Gravis
The nurse is caring for a client diagnosed 
with Guillain-Barré syndrome (GBS) 
following a severe viral infection. Which 
classification of medication should the 
nurse anticipate the health care provider 
will prescribe?
A. Neuromuscular blocking agents
B. Corticosteroids
C. Cholinergic muscle stimulants
D. immunoglobulin (IVIG)
The answers are: A, C, and E. Risk factors for 
developing Guillain-Barré Syndrome include: 
experiencing upper respiratory infection, GI 
infection (especially from Campylobacter 
Jejuni), Epstein-Barr infection, HIV/AIDS, 
vaccination (flu or swine flu) etc.
NCLE X Style Questions
D.IVIG treats Guillain-Barré 
syndrome by reducing the immune 
system’s attack on peripheral 
nerves, limiting nerve damage and 
helping recovery.
